title: Foundation
short: Build the habits every algorithm needs.
idea: An algorithm is a precise sequence of decisions. Before reaching for a clever technique, define what the input means, what the result should be, and what must stay true after each step.
invariant: After visiting the first i elements, your running answer is correct for exactly those elements.
explain: Start with a small example and compute the answer by hand. Include an empty input if the contract allows it, a single element, duplicates, and negative values.
A running sum, minimum, or maximum is a compressed summary of the prefix you have already seen. Update it once for each element.
Big O describes how work grows with input size. One pass over n items is O(n); repeatedly halving a search interval is O(log n). Memory counts extra storage, separate from the input.
pitfall: Do not initialize a maximum to zero when all inputs may be negative. Use the first element or the lowest representable value.
quiz: A loop visits each of n items once and keeps only a running sum. What is its extra space?
why: The number of stored variables does not grow with n.

title: Arrays
short: Read, write, and rearrange with intention.
idea: An array stores values by index. Most array problems become simpler when you decide which part is already processed and what summary you need to keep.
invariant: Every processed position satisfies the desired property; unprocessed values remain available.
explain: Random access lets you read an index in O(1), but inserting in the middle of a contiguous array may shift O(n) elements.
Use a read pointer to inspect values and a write pointer to build a valid prefix. The write pointer never needs to overtake the reader.
In the water lab, a position traps min(left maximum, right maximum) minus its height. Advancing the lower boundary makes that position’s water level knowable without scanning the other side again.
pitfall: In-place algorithms overwrite data. Before writing, check whether a later step still needs the old value.
quiz: Why can the water algorithm process the smaller boundary?
options: The opposite boundary is already tall enough
why: The lower side limits the water level, so a higher boundary on the other side cannot increase it.

title: Linked List
short: Make pointers feel less like magic.
idea: A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node owns a value and a reference to the next node. Changing a reference changes the shape of the chain.
invariant: prev points to the reversed prefix; curr points to the untouched suffix.
explain: Reversing a list requires saving curr.next before changing it. Otherwise the remaining chain becomes unreachable.
On every iteration, redirect curr.next toward prev, then advance both pointers. Each node moves from the untouched suffix into the reversed prefix.
Dummy nodes simplify insertions and deletions at the head. Fast and slow pointers detect cycles or locate a middle without knowing the length.
pitfall: Compare node identities when finding an intersection. Equal values do not mean the two lists share a node.
quiz: What must you save before reversing curr.next?
why: Saving next preserves access to the part of the chain you have not reversed.

title: Strings
short: Turn characters into counts and structure.
idea: A string is a sequence, but the right representation often matters more than the sequence itself: a frequency map, a last-seen index, or a normalized character stream.
invariant: The active window contains no repeated character.
explain: For anagrams, ordering is irrelevant and counts are everything. Matching frequency maps gives a direct correctness argument.
For substring questions, track a contiguous interval. Expand the right end, then shrink the left end until the condition becomes valid again.
Decide whether the task means ASCII characters, Unicode code points, or user-perceived graphemes. JavaScript indexing uses UTF-16 code units; Python iterates code points.
pitfall: When a repeated character appears before the current left boundary, do not move left backward.
quiz: For “abba”, after seeing the last a, should the left boundary move back to 1?
why: The last a is outside the active window. Use max(left, lastSeen + 1).

title: Stack and Queues
short: Choose which item gets handled next.
idea: A stack handles the most recently added item first. A queue handles the oldest item first. That small difference shapes parsing, undo history, and breadth-first exploration.
invariant: The stack contains exactly the opening brackets not yet matched.
explain: Push an opening bracket. For a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener. An empty stack or a different opener makes the sequence invalid.
A monotonic stack keeps values in a useful order. When a new value breaks that order, popped items can receive their final answers.
A queue drives BFS by processing nodes in discovery order. Use a deque or a moving head index rather than repeatedly removing the first element of an array.
pitfall: A sequence may finish without a mismatch but still contain unmatched openers. Check that the stack is empty.
quiz: Which item leaves a queue first?
why: Queues follow first in, first out.

title: Binary Search Algorithm
short: Throw away half, with a proof.
idea: Binary search works when a comparison lets you rule out an entire region. Sorted arrays are one example; any monotone true/false condition can define a searchable boundary.
invariant: If the target exists, it lies in the current inclusive interval [lo, hi].
explain: Inspect the middle. If its value is too small, every value to its left is also too small, so set lo to mid + 1.
If its value is too large, set hi to mid − 1. Removing mid guarantees that each unsuccessful comparison shrinks the interval.
For first-true problems, keep the answer as a candidate and continue searching to the left. For rotated arrays, first identify which half remains sorted.
pitfall: Choose inclusive or half-open bounds and use them consistently. Compute mid as lo + (hi − lo) / 2 to avoid fixed-width addition overflow.
quiz: After one failed comparison in a sorted array, how much of the remaining interval can usually be discarded?
why: The middle comparison orders all elements on one side relative to the target.

title: Two Pointers & Sliding Window
short: Trade repeated work for moving boundaries.
idea: Two pointers summarize a pair of positions or an interval. When each boundary moves in only one direction, nested-looking loops can still do only linear work.
invariant: All discarded positions have already been proved irrelevant or fully processed.
explain: On a sorted array, a pair sum below the target can only improve by increasing the left value. A sum above the target can only improve by decreasing the right value.
For windows, adding and removing one element should update your summary cheaply. Counts, sums, and deques are common summaries.
The total movement is what matters: if left and right each advance at most n times, the full process is O(n), even when one loop appears inside another.
pitfall: A sum-based variable window does not automatically work with negative numbers: expanding may decrease the sum and shrinking may increase it.
quiz: Both pointers move forward at most n times. What is their total movement?
why: Add the number of movements of each pointer. They do not multiply.

title: Binary Tree
short: Solve a node, trust the smaller trees.
idea: A binary tree gives each node at most two children. Recursive algorithms work by solving the left and right subtrees, then combining their answers at the current node.
invariant: When a recursive call returns, its result is correct for the entire subtree it was given.
explain: Preorder visits node, left, right. Inorder visits left, node, right. Postorder visits left, right, node. The visit position controls when you combine information.
BFS uses a queue to process one level at a time. Capture the queue length at the start of a level to avoid mixing in newly discovered children.
For depth, return 1 + max(left depth, right depth). For diameter, consider left depth + right depth at each node while returning only depth to the parent.
pitfall: A deeply skewed tree has height n. Recursive extra space can be O(n), not always O(log n).
quiz: Which traversal visits the root after both children?
why: Postorder completes both subtrees before visiting their parent.

title: Binary Search Tree
short: Use order to choose the next branch.
idea: A binary search tree places smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right subtree. This is a rule for every descendant, not only immediate children.
invariant: Every node must lie inside the value bounds inherited from all of its ancestors.
explain: To search, compare with the current node and follow just one branch. The cost is O(h), where h is the tree height.
Inorder traversal produces sorted keys. This supports kth-smallest selection and an alternative validation strategy.
Validation passes a lower and upper bound down the tree. A left child inherits a new upper bound; a right child inherits a new lower bound.
pitfall: An ordinary BST is not automatically balanced. Its worst-case search time is O(n).
quiz: Is checking only each node’s immediate children sufficient to validate a BST?
why: A descendant may obey its parent while violating the ordering required by an earlier ancestor.

title: Heap
short: Keep the next priority within reach.
idea: A heap is a nearly complete tree with a local order rule. In a max heap, every parent is at least as large as its children. The root is therefore the maximum.
invariant: Every parent has priority at least as high as its children.
explain: In an array-backed zero-indexed heap, children of i are 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The parent is floor((i − 1) / 2).
Insertion sifts a new value upward. Removing the root replaces it with the final value, then sifts it downward. Both operations take O(log n).
To retain the largest k values, use a min heap of size k. Its root is the smallest retained candidate, ready to replace when a better value arrives.
pitfall: A heap is partially ordered. Reading its backing array does not produce a fully sorted sequence.
quiz: Which heap keeps the largest k values with the weakest candidate at the root?
options: A min heap of size k
A max heap of size n
why: The minimum of the retained values is exactly the candidate to remove next.

title: Backtracking
idea: Backtracking explores a decision tree. Build one partial answer, try a choice, recurse, then undo the choice so the next branch starts from the same state.
invariant: The current path contains exactly the choices made along the active recursion branch.
explain: For subsets, every element has two choices: skip it or include it. That produces 2ⁿ leaves.
Prune only when a partial choice cannot lead to a valid answer. In a positive-number combination sum, a remaining target below zero cannot recover.
When duplicates exist, sort first and skip equivalent choices at the same recursion depth. Copy a path when saving it so later mutations do not alter saved answers.
pitfall: Forgetting to undo a choice leaks state into sibling branches. Saving the same mutable list repeatedly is another common error.
quiz: How many subsets does a set of n distinct elements have?
why: Each element independently has two possible decisions: included or excluded.

title: Greedy Algorithm
short: Make a local choice you can defend.
idea: A greedy algorithm commits to a locally attractive choice. It needs a reason that this choice can be part of some optimal solution; speed alone is not a proof.
invariant: The chosen intervals are compatible, and the last end time is as small as possible for the chosen count.
explain: For interval scheduling, choose the interval that finishes earliest. It leaves at least as much room for future intervals as any other first choice.
An exchange argument replaces the first interval in an optimal schedule with the earliest-finishing one. This replacement cannot make later intervals impossible.
Greedy rules are problem-specific. Earliest finish is correct for maximizing a compatible count, while merging overlapping intervals usually sorts by start instead.
pitfall: A rule that works for one interval problem may fail for a weighted version. Weighted interval scheduling needs a different method.
quiz: For the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals, which ordering supports the greedy choice?
why: Finishing early preserves the most room for later compatible intervals.

title: Dynamic Programming
idea: Dynamic programming defines a small state, writes a recurrence, and evaluates each state once. The hard part is deciding what information makes the future independent of the past.
invariant: Before computing dp[i], every smaller state used by its recurrence is already correct.
explain: Climbing stairs asks how many ways reach step i with moves of one or two. The final move comes from i − 1 or i − 2, so ways[i] = ways[i − 1] + ways[i − 2].
Set base cases before the loop: there is one way to stand at step 0, and one way to reach step 1.
Memoization caches recursive answers. Tabulation fills states in dependency order. If only two prior states are needed, replace the table with two variables.
pitfall: Loop order can change meaning. In coin change, counting combinations and counting ordered sequences need different outer loops.
quiz: If dp[i] uses only dp[i−1] and dp[i−2], how much extra space is necessary?
why: Two rolling values preserve every dependency needed by the next state.

title: Graphs
idea: A graph models vertices and their connections. BFS explores in distance layers; DFS follows a branch before returning. A visited set prevents repeated exploration.
invariant: Each discovered vertex is enqueued once, and its BFS distance is the shortest number of edges from the source.
explain: An adjacency list stores neighbors for each vertex. Traversing every vertex and edge takes O(V + E).
Mark a vertex visited when you enqueue it, not when you remove it. Otherwise multiple neighbors may enqueue the same vertex.
BFS finds shortest paths when every edge has equal cost. For nonnegative unequal weights, use Dijkstra’s algorithm. Topological order exists only for directed acyclic graphs.
pitfall: In an undirected graph, an edge back to your parent is not a cycle. In a directed graph, use an active recursion set to distinguish a back edge from a completed node.
quiz: When does ordinary BFS guarantee shortest paths?
why: BFS processes layers by number of edges. Equal edge costs make those layers cost-optimal.
